results.title: Introducing the Oracle OCCL Network Plugin for Reliable Distributed AI Workloads | cloud-infrastructure
results.author: Lilian Quan
highlights:
# Introducing the OCCL Network Plugin for Reliable Distributed AI Workloads

 November 6, 2026 5 minute read

...

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) is introducing Oracle Collective Communications Library (OCCL) network plugin, a collective-communication network plugin designed for distributed AI workloads on OCI-supported GPUs and remote direct memory access (RDMA)-enabled AI infrastructure. OCCL works with NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and AMD Radeon Collective Communications Library (RCCL) to provide congestion-aware traffic distribution across available network planes and automatic recovery from supported link and NIC failures. It does this through the standard NCCL/RCCL network-plugin interface, without requiring changes to customer training applications, AI frameworks, or collective-communication calls.

...

# Availability and next steps

The OCCL network plugin is generally available at no additional charge for customers using supported OCI GPU and RDMA-enabled AI infrastructure. Customers continue to pay the standard OCI charges for GPU compute, networking, storage, and applicable support services. Customers can use Oracle HPC images for the preinstalled experience or use the open-source distribution for supported custom images.

results.title: How to Optimize AI Inference Costs
results.author: Michelle Meng
highlights:
# How to Reduce AI Inference Costs Without Hurting Performance

Michelle Meng | Product Marketing Director for GenAI | October 7, 2026

...

- AI inference costs should be measured per useful outcome as well as per request, token, or GPU-hour.
- The largest cost drivers are model complexity, workload demand, and infrastructure efficiency.
- Optimization should begin with baselines for cost, quality, latency, and throughput.
- Several techniques can lower unit cost, but each has tradeoffs.
- Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) offers managed inference for generative AI and dedicated AI infrastructure for teams that need cost-effective, predictable capacity and high-throughput performance.

...

Costs are coming down in some areas, but lower unit prices don't eliminate the need to optimize inference costs. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index Report found that organizational AI adoption reached 88% in 2025 as growth of frontier models accelerated. Those figures point to broader production use and a rapidly expanding model ecosystem, both of which can increase total inference demand even as the costs of some model calls fall. Production spending can still rise when usage levels and workflow complexity grow faster than price declines.

...

### On-Demand vs. Dedicated AI Inference: Which Costs Less?

On-demand inference often costs less for experimentation or workloads with unpredictable demand. It usually charges by request, character, token, or transaction, so spending follows usage more closely.

Dedicated inference can cost less for workloads with steady utilization and strict operating requirements. The tradeoff is commitment: Teams pay for reserved capacity and need enough useful work to justify that investment.

OCI Enterprise AI supports both on-demand inference and Dedicated AI Clusters. On-demand inference uses pay-as-you-go pricing for inference calls, while Dedicated AI Clusters provide dedicated GPU capacity for supported model hosting and fine-tuning, with usage commitments that depend on the model and cluster type.

...

Improve AI Inference Price-Performance with Oracle

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives teams several paths for improving AI inference price-performance, including managed generative AI services and GPU infrastructure for custom serving stacks. OCI Enterprise AI supports on-demand inference for pay-as-you-go usage and Dedicated AI Clusters for predictable pricing and dedicated capacity when teams need to host foundation or fine-tuned models.

The OCI Enterprise AI Model Import feature can also help teams optimize inference costs by letting them import open-weight models with different sizes, capabilities, and performance characteristics. Teams can select and deploy a model that meets the quality requirements of a workload without using more model capability than the task requires, helping balance inference cost and application performance.

For teams running large models or high-volume inference, OCI AI infrastructure provides GPU resources and high performance networking for training and inference workloads. These capabilities matter when cost depends on keeping accelerators busy, moving data quickly, and matching infrastructure to model size and latency requirements.

results.title: Introducing Dynamic Resource Virtual Machines | cloud-infrastructure
results.author: Chris Manolarakis
highlights:
# Introducing Dynamic Resource Virtual Machines

 October 14, 2026 4 minute read 

Chris Manolarakis

Principal Product Manager

Application resource demand changes over time with traffic, business activity, scheduled processing, and other workload patterns. Customers typically configure compute and memory capacity to support periods of peak demand. When demand is lower, the same workloads can remain overprovisioned because their configured capacity stays the same while actual resource use declines.

...

Today, we are excited to announce the general availability of Dynamic Resource Virtual Machines (DRVM) for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Compute. DRVM gives customers a more efficient and economical way to maintain the OCPU and memory capacity their applications require while OCI dynamically manages the physical resources backing each VM.

DRVM is available for eligible VM.Standard.E6.Flex configurations in select OCI regions, with additional OCI Compute shapes and regions planned in the following months.

The preceding is intended to outline our general product direction, It is intended for information purposes only, and may not be incorporated into any contract. It is not a commitment to deliver any material, code or functionality, and should not be relied upon in making purchasing decisions. The development, release, timing and pricing of any features or functionality described for Oracle’s products may change and remains at the sole discretion of Oracle Corporation.

...

## DRVM economics

DRVM instances receive a 10% discount on their OCPU and memory usage. For example, an E6 Flex VM configured with 8 OCPUs and 64 GB of memory using dynamic resource management receives the same configured OCPU and memory capacity at a 10% lower cost than the equivalent Standard E6 Flex configuration. Storage, networking, operating-system licenses, and other separately billed services retain their applicable rates.

 October 27, 2026 6 minute read

AMD Helios is an open, co-designed AI infrastructure platform aligned with the Open Compute Project Open Rack Wide design. It integrates 72 AMD Instinct™ MI455X GPUs across 18 four-GPU compute trays, alongside 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ “Venice” CPUs, AMD Pensando networking, and AMD ROCm™ software. ...

In October 2025, Oracle announced general availability of OCI Compute with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, following its launch of MI300X-based instances in 2024. For customers, the goal is more useful AI output, responsive inference, and better workload economics. Cost per token or completed workloads provide a practical way to assess that value against each application’s performance requirements. AMD Helios brings GPU capacity, HBM4 memory, communication, and open software together. AMD Pensando-based Oracle Acceleron SmartNICs support efficient, secure infrastructure services, while E7 provides CPU capacity for the applications and agent workflows surrounding the model.

results.title: Accelerate AI data access on OCI with Alluxio | cloud-infrastructure
results.author: Pinkesh Valdria
highlights:
# Accelerate AI data access on OCI with Alluxio

 October 6, 2026 8 minute read 

Pinkesh Valdria

Director - AI/ML/GPU/Storage Infra Specialist Team (Global)

Bin Fan Founder and VP, Technology Alluxio, Inc.

Enterprises investing in artificial intelligence and machine learning infrastructure often seek to improve price performance by increasing GPU utilization while managing infrastructure and data-access costs.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) provides high-performance GPU compute for demanding AI workloads. For I/O-intensive workloads, however, latency and bandwidth between compute and remote object storage can affect overall accelerator utilization. When GPUs wait for data, organizations may pay for accelerator capacity that is not being fully used.

This reference architecture shows how deploying Alluxio as a compute-side distributed caching layer on OCI can help:

- Improve GPU utilization
- Reduce effective infrastructure cost for certain training or inference workloads
- Reduce data-access latency for frequently accessed datasets
- Work with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Object Storage and other supported object-storage backends

By helping reduce storage-related bottlenecks, this architecture can help improve effective GPU price performance for supported workloads.

## Business objective: Improve AI infrastructure price performance

GPU clusters can represent a significant component of AI infrastructure cost. Price performance can improve when:

- GPUs maintain higher utilization
- I/O bottlenecks are reduced
- Unnecessary remote data movement is reduced
- Persistent storage remains cost-efficient

Adding Alluxio on the compute side can help keep GPUs supplied with frequently accessed data more consistently, supporting improved utilization and infrastructure efficiency.

...

### Co-located mode: Cost-efficient configuration

Alluxio runs on the provisioned GPU instances.

Potential fit:

- Smaller clusters
- Rapid deployment
- Cost-sensitive environments

Potential benefits:

- Does not require separate caching nodes
- Can use existing local NVMe capacity
- Uses configurable CPU, memory, and NVMe resources alongside the GPU workload
- Can help improve price performance in appropriate compact environments

...

## Performance characteristics

Benchmark results discussed in this post include:

- Approximately 90–98% accelerator utilization reported by MLPerf Storage v2.0 using emulated H100 accelerators. [1] 
- Approximately 0.3–0.6 ms average warm-cache data-access latency measured with WARP
- Up to approximately 57 GB/s aggregate I/O throughput measured in the six-node MLPerf Storage configuration using 100 Gbps networking

The key takeaway is that reducing time spent waiting for frequently accessed data can help increase sustained GPU utilization and improve effective GPU price performance for I/O-constrained workloads. See the related OCI + Alluxio benchmark article.

## Price-performance impact

Without a compute-side cache, I/O-constrained workloads may experience:

- More GPU time waiting for remote reads
- Higher effective infrastructure cost for a given amount of useful accelerator work

With an appropriately configured Alluxio cache:

- GPUs can spend less time waiting for repeatedly accessed data
- Repeated remote-storage access, and associated access costs where applicable, may be reduced
- Higher infrastructure utilization can help improve effective price performance

### Performance comparison

| Metric | Baseline | Alluxio | Improvement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Illustrative GPU utilization* | 60% | 95% | 58% higher |
| WARP benchmark — 10 KiB objects, high-frequency small-object access | | | |
| Average latency (16 concurrent connections) | 24.1 ms | 0.45 ms | ~53X lower |
| IOPS (48 concurrent connections, 6-node cluster) | 11,800 | 240,800 | ~20X |
| WARP benchmark — 1 GiB objects, ~500 GB dataset | | | |
| Throughput | 6.5 GiB/s | 33.3 GiB/s average (40.9 GiB/s peak) | ~5X |

...

By deploying Alluxio as a compute-side caching layer with OCI GPU instances, organizations can help reduce data-access latency, improve accelerator utilization, and improve effective price performance for appropriately configured I/O-constrained workloads.
